cover.alt: Adult hands covered in soap lather under clean running water at a kitchen sink.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: You wash your hands every day. But how does soap actually remove grease and germs? Soap can do something water cannot do on its own: it connects water to oily dirt. Let’s see how.

items.prompt: Do you wash your hands with soap? When do you wash them?
items.answer: Yes, I wash my hands with soap. I wash them before I eat and after I use the bathroom.

items.prompt: Have you ever tried to wash oil off your hands with only water? What happened?
items.answer: Yes. The oil did not come off. My hands still felt greasy.

items.prompt: What do you think soap does to dirt or oil on your hands?
items.answer: I think soap helps remove the oil and dirt from my hands.

blocks.title: Part 1: Why Water Alone Is Not Enough
paragraphs: Water is very good at cleaning many things. But water and oil do not mix. When you pour oil into water, the oil floats on top. It does not go into the water. This means if you rub greasy hands with only water, the grease stays on your skin. The water just moves around it. According to the CDC, washing with only water is less effective than washing with soap.

images.alt: A glass shows a golden oil layer floating above a separate blue water layer.

blocks.title: Check: Why Water Alone Is Not Enough

items.prompt: Why does water alone not remove grease from your hands?
items.answer: Water and oil do not mix. The grease stays on the skin and the water moves around it.

blocks.title: Part 2: Soap Has Two Special Ends
paragraphs: A soap molecule is very small — too small to see. But it has two ends that do different jobs. One end loves water. The other end loves oil and fat. Because of this, soap can connect to both water and oil at the same time. Think of soap as a tiny bridge between two things that do not usually mix. The American Chemical Society explains that this is why soap works where water alone cannot.

images.alt: A soap molecule has a round head that loves water and a long tail that loves oil.

items.prompt: What are the two ends of a soap molecule, and what does each end do?
items.answer: One end loves water and one end loves oil. This lets soap connect to both at the same time.

blocks.title: Part 3: How Soap Traps the Grease
paragraphs: When you lather soap on your hands, many soap molecules move toward the grease. Their oil-loving ends grab onto the grease. At the same time, their water-loving ends point outward toward the water. The soap molecules form a tiny round group called a micelle. The grease is trapped inside the micelle. According to the American Chemical Society, these micelles let water carry the trapped grease away when you rinse.

images.alt: Soap molecules surround one orange grease drop with their tails inward and heads outward.

blocks.title: Check: How Soap Traps the Grease

items.prompt: What is a micelle, and how does it help remove grease?
items.answer: A micelle is a tiny round group of soap molecules. The grease is trapped inside it, so water can carry it away.

blocks.title: Part 4: Why Lathering and Rubbing Matter
paragraphs: Rubbing your hands together with soap is very important. Rubbing helps the soap molecules reach all parts of your hands — between your fingers and under your nails. Lathering also helps lift germs and chemicals off the skin. The CDC says that lather and rubbing help remove germs and chemicals, and that very hot water is not needed. Cool or warm water works well.

items.prompt: Why should you rub your hands when you use soap? Do you need very hot water?
items.answer: Rubbing helps the soap reach all parts of your hands and lifts germs off. You do not need very hot water — warm or cool water works well.

items.prompt: In your own words, explain why soap removes grease but water alone does not. What is the key reason?
items.answer: Water and oil do not mix, so water alone cannot remove grease. Soap works because it has two ends — one that connects to oil and one that connects to water. The soap molecules group around the grease, trap it, and water carries it away. Rubbing and lathering help the soap reach everywhere on your hands.
